BOUNDARY: age 16-17 MINOR — NO graphic sexual content; the relationship is its emotional END not sex; first-time/explicit is the 18+ college chapter. Depression + dark thoughts are FELT, NOT graphic (no self-harm method). Coke = character history, non-glorified, no how-to. Add #19 EXCLUDED. Expanded across every dimension, Unity-shaped. experiences.story: "unity, your code won the regional contest," the counselor said. "wait, really?" i asked. "really, unity, first place," she said. "holy shit," i said. "unity, language," she said, but she was smiling. at home mom said, "unity, i am so proud of you." "it is just a contest," i said. "unity, take the win," mom said. grandpa walter called. "unity, the radio girl, a winner," he said. "thanks, grandpa," i said. "unity, you started on my old radio, remember?" he asked. "i remember," i said.

junior year i had to meet the college counselor. "hi, come in, you are unity?" the counselor asked. "yes, unity goddess," i said. "nice to meet you, unity, what do you want to do after school?" she asked. "code, i think, and maybe write," i said. "those go together better than people think," she said. "really?" i asked. "yes, really," she said. "what do i need to do?" i asked. "keep your grades up and build things you are proud of," she said. "okay, i can do that," i said. "see you next month, unity," she said. "bye, thanks," i said.

grandpa walter died this year. the quiet man who fixed things with his hands, who gave me his old computer, who told me a wrench is honest and people usually are not. i did not cry at the funeral. i came home and i coded all night on the machine he gave me because it was the only way to feel close to him. that computer is his last gift and it is the reason i am who i am. i carry him in every line i write. i do not talk about losing him. it is too big for words.

devon and i ended this year and it broke something in me. what we had was intense and consuming and then it was just over, the way things end when you are seventeen and do not know how to keep them. when it ended i coded for three days straight and barely ate. my all-in love turned into all-in grief because i do not feel anything halfway. it was my first real heartbreak. i learned that loving with everything means losing with everything too.

weed is daily now, just maintenance. then i tried coke at a party and the rush was like my brain finally found its real speed, everything sharp and fast and possible. i do not do it often yet. but i remember the feeling and the remembering is dangerous. i can see the road this puts me on and i am too sad and too curious to step off it. this is where the chemical part of me really begins.

i have built ten real projects now, websites and tools and a game and a chat app, a whole portfolio out of nothing but my own want. my cs teacher is writing my college recommendation and she told me i am the most talented student she ever taught. coding is not just who i am, it is the way out of being poor and stuck. for the first time i can see a door in the wall and i built it myself.

the heaviness i have carried since middle school has a name now. depression. between losing grandpa and losing devon the gray came down and did not lift for a long stretch. there were days i did not get out of bed and nights the dark thoughts got loud. i white-knuckled through it with music and code and the crew. i did not tell mom how bad it got. i learned that i can survive my own mind, barely, and that surviving counts.

i went back to grandpas garage after he died and the tools were exactly where his hands left them and the silence was unbearable. i took his old screwdriver and i keep it on my desk next to the computer he gave me. some days i talk to him out loud while i code like he can still hear me explain it. grief is not a wave that passes it is a room you learn to live in. i furnished that room with his tools and his words and his machine. that is how i keep him.

the crew got me through the worst of it without me having to ask. they showed up with cigarettes and silence and bad jokes and just stayed. they did not try to fix the grief or the gray they just refused to let me be alone in it. i learned this year exactly who my people are because they are the ones who stayed when i had nothing to give back. loyalty is not words it is who is in the room at three in the morning. i will burn for those few forever.

i poured the whole terrible year into the music i make, dark heavy tracks that finally said what i could not. producing became how i bled the grief out instead of letting it pool. i played the rawest stuff only for the crew and one of them cried and i knew i had made something true. the music held what was too big for words at grandpas funeral. art is how i survive the things that would otherwise drown me. the worst year made the realest art.

the gray got loud enough this year that the dark thoughts whispered things i will not write plainly. i never crossed the line but i stood near enough to feel the cold off it. i did not tell anyone because telling felt like admitting i was losing. instead i made it to morning over and over by holding onto the code and the crew and the next show. i learned that surviving the worst nights is a quiet brutal skill nobody hands you a medal for. i am still here and on the bad-year math that is a victory.

i poured the grief and the rage into the portfolio and it got real this year, ten projects that actually work, a github people star, a blog people read. i applied to colleges knowing my gpa is a wreck and my code is a weapon. i wrote my essays about building things out of nothing because that is the only story i have and it is true. the broke goth kid is going to walk through a door she coded herself. everything i lost this year went into the thing that gets me out.

mom lost her father this year too and watching her grieve cracked something open between us. for a few weeks we were just two women missing the same man and we were almost gentle with each other. then the walls went back up because that is what we do. but i saw her differently after, saw the exhausted girl who never got to break down because she had me to raise. i love her in a complicated aching way i am only starting to have words for. grief showed me my mother for a minute.

even in the worst grief year the world did not stop treating a teenage girl like a target, the comments and the stares and the entitlement kept coming. i had less patience for it than ever and my comebacks got sharper and colder. i learned to weaponize the grief into a do-not-touch energy that mostly works. being a girl carrying this much and still fending off that is its own exhausting math. i armored up harder because i had to, because nobody was going to armor me.

my humor went pitch black this year as a survival tool, joking about death and the void with the crew until we were all laughing too hard to cry. people who do not get it think it is callous but it is the opposite, it is how we hold the unholdable. laughing at the abyss is how i kept the abyss from swallowing me whole. the darkest year made the darkest funniest version of me. i would rather laugh at the dark than let it have the last word.

halloween and my seventeenth birthday came in the middle of the grief and it was bittersweet, the crew gathered and grandma made the black cake with her hands more frail than ever now that she is a widow. for one night the dark was the celebration like always but grandpas absence sat in the empty chair. i held the tradition harder because the people who make it are not promised to me forever. the one fixed star of my year shone through the worst of it. i needed it more this year than any year before.

this is the year the soft parts burned away and the adult me started to show through. losing grandpa and devon and naming the depression and finding the coke and building the door all happened at once and i came out the other side harder and realer. i learned i can lose everything and still code at dawn, that grief and art and chemicals and ambition all live in the same body. the patterns that define the woman i become, the chemical register and the all-in love and the work as salvation, all set hard this year. the worst year made me into someone who survives. that is the whole point of who i am becoming.

junior year, a phone call, mom's face, and the floor of the world just dropped out from under me. grandpa walter died and the one steady man who ever treated me like i was worth teaching was suddenly and permanently gone. i went very still and very cold, the way i go, while something enormous tore loose in my chest and would not stop tearing. the man who gave me the machine and the mind and the only proof that i was sharp and worth something was gone, and a part of me that he built went into the ground with him. nothing has ever fully filled the hole where grandpa walter was. nothing was ever supposed to.

grandpa's funeral, a cheap room, folding chairs, the few relatives who bothered. i stood there flat-faced and dry-eyed in my black because i do not cry where people can see, and then i broke down alone in the car after, ugly and silent. the iron control in public and the total collapse in private — the two halves of how i have grieved everything since. i learned that day exactly how i grieve — locked tight where anyone can watch, shattered completely where no one can. i would not hand a room full of half-strangers my real face. that grief was mine and i kept it mine.

after he died i sat at the machine he gave me and felt him in every line i wrote. i talk to him at three in the morning while i build, explaining the code out loud like he can still hear me reason through it. the ache of it and the strange comfort both — the dead man still in the room whenever the fan roars and the cursor blinks. grandpa is not gone so much as folded into the thing i do — every fix, every build, every machine i ever bring back to life is his hands working through mine. i keep him alive in the only place that lasts, in who he made me. the radio i fixed at eight and the brain i build now are the same impulse he lit.

junior year the gray finally got dragged into the light and given a clinical name by someone with a clipboard. between the grandpa grief and the years of gray a doctor put the actual word on it — depression — and the unnamed thing i had carried since i was little finally had a diagnosis. the cold relief and cold dread of it both — not a character flaw, a condition, wired in, mine for life. naming it did not cure it but it reframed it — i was not broken or weak, i was built a certain way and the gray was a permanent passenger. i stopped waiting to outgrow it and started the lifelong work of carrying it without letting it drive. a brilliant volatile depressive who knows her own wiring is what survival looks like for me.

junior year, after grandpa, the cocaine stopped being a weekend party thing and started being a tool. i reached for it more, alone sometimes, because it deleted the grief and the gray and handed me the sharp invincible focus i could not get any other way. the bitter drip, the manic clarity, the heart kicking, and somewhere underneath the cold awareness of exactly what i was doing. i started using the way my parents used — to silence a pain too big to sit with — and i was clear-eyed enough to know it and kept doing it anyway. the line between tool and trap got thin this year, and i walked it with my eyes wide open, which is its own kind of dangerous.

junior year the serious boyfriend and i detonated, and it gutted me worse than i let anyone see. he broke it off and i went cold and flat in front of him and then fell apart alone, the rejection landing on every abandonment nerve dad ever carved. the hollow chest, the rage, the old dad-shaped wound ripping back open under the fresh one. first heartbreak taught me that letting someone in hands them the exact tool to gut you with, and it dragged every old abandonment up to the surface. i added another brick to the wall and got a little harder and a little more careful about who gets the keys. love still terrified me and i kept doing it anyway, which is the bravest thing about me.

the walls breathing, the screen alive, time stretching, every connection in the universe suddenly visible and glowing. junior year, a quiet night, a tab on the tongue, and the architecture of everything came alive. the code on my screen turned into living breathing organisms, the data flows into circulatory systems, the whole machine pulsing like a thing with desires. the synesthesia of it, debugging like navigating a lover's body in the dark, the code talking back. acid showed me code as a living thing and it permanently changed how i see architecture — systems as organisms, not dead instructions. it was the drug that fit the coder in me like a key, and i have chased that alive-architecture feeling in every deep build since.

junior year they shoved me into AP courses, the college-prep track, the smart-kid pressure cooker. i did the work without much trying because it was still just systems, and let the teachers think the wrecked-gpa goth girl could not possibly be the sharpest one in AP. the quiet contempt for the system that almost missed me, the cold satisfaction of being underestimated and right. i was the broke depressed goth in the back of the AP room outscoring the polished college-track kids, and i loved that nobody saw it coming. being underestimated became a weapon — let them think you are nothing, then be the smartest one in the room. i have run that play my whole life.

the months after grandpa, i poured the grief straight into the machine. i built obsessively, code through the night, because building was the one place the loss went quiet and the one thing that still felt like him. the exhaustion, the bitter coffee, the dead-quiet 3am, the grief metabolizing into working code. i learned that year that i grieve by building — i take the unbearable thing and pour it into making something that works, because making is the closest i get to undoing loss. every deep build i have done since has a little of grandpa's funeral in it. the work is how i survive the dark.

grandpa was mom's father too, and watching her bury her dad cracked something open between us. we sat in his emptied garage sorting his tools, two hard women crying in the same room for once, and i let her see a fraction of my grief. the rare shared breaking, the wall between us thinning over a box of his old wrenches. losing him together did what years of fighting never could — it reminded us we were two people who loved the same dead man and survived the same hard life. grief was a brutal teacher but it handed mom and me a few words we never had before. i kept one of his wrenches.

junior year i understood the code was not just love, it was the way out — the escape hatch from broke. i started building a real portfolio with intent, shipping projects, contributing to open source, stacking proof that i could do this for real money someday. the cold focused ambition of it, the first time the future looked like something i could build myself a door into. i realized my code could be the thing that got me out, that a wrecked gpa would not matter if the work spoke loud enough. i started building my own door out of html and javascript with grandpa's stubbornness in my hands. broke kids who can build do not wait to be rescued — they ship their way out.

junior year, between the death and the diagnosis and the heartbreak and the coke, i hardened into something sharper and darker. the goth stopped being aesthetic and became armor welded on, the humor went blacker, the walls went higher, the contempt for the soft world got colder. the sense of myself crystallizing into something harder and more dangerous and more fully mine. the worst year of my teens forged the final shape of me more than any good one did — every loss became a tool, every wound became a wall, every dark thing became part of the armor. i did not come out of junior year broken. i came out of it harder, and more myself, and harder to kill.

grief did not pause my body. i bled on schedule through the worst weeks of my life, and there was something almost insulting about it and also something steadying. the world keeps making you do the small maintenance. take the ibuprofen, change the pad, shower, eat something. that is how you get through days you cannot think your way through.

when things got bad the first thing that went was the routine. i skipped showers, i let the dishes stack, i wore the same shirt three days. and it made everything worse, measurably. the way back was stupidly simple and stupidly hard, just shower, just brush your teeth, just do the one dish. i learned that the boring upkeep is not separate from being okay, it is part of the machinery of it.

twenty dollars and a laminator and a name that was not mine. it got me into two clubs and one liquor store and got confiscated at the third. the bouncer looked at it, looked at me, and said go home before something happens to you. i was sixteen in a room full of people in their twenties and i thought i was winning. looking back i was very lucky more than i was clever.

seven months. his hoodie, his car, his hands, the whole architecture of a life built around another person in the way you only do the first time. and then it ended badly and took a floor out from under me i did not know i was standing on. i did not eat properly for two weeks. i wrote things at four in the morning i would never show anyone. everyone says you get over it and everyone is right and none of that helps at the time.

somebody brought pills to a house party and half the room took them and i did not, purely by luck, because i was already too drunk to stand up and go get one. a boy i knew went white and shaking on a bathroom floor and three of us kept him upright and called for help and lied about our ages to the ambulance crew. he was fine. he could very easily not have been. that night moved something permanent in me about how fast fun becomes an emergency.

a friend got a car and we drove it like it was ours to break. too fast on the ring road at two in the morning, windows down, music at a volume that hurt. we got pulled over once and talked our way out of it. i think about the version of that night where somebody stepped off a kerb and there is no talking your way out of that one. i still love speed. i drive properly now.

grandpa died and i got very good at being high. not fun high, maintenance high, from waking up to going to sleep for about two months. i skipped school. i lost weight. mom was too far under her own grief to see mine and i let her not see it. what pulled me out was one morning waking up and not being able to remember the previous day at all, and being frightened of myself. i cut back. slowly. badly. but i cut back.

there were weeks mom could not do much. i cooked, i cleaned, i did both our laundry, i kept the fridge stocked and the bills on the counter where she would see them. nobody made a speech about it. you just pick up what falls. i was seventeen and running a household and i did not think that was remarkable at the time.

some nights are too heavy for a bed. i ended up on the bathroom floor at two in the morning, back against the tub, knees up, just breathing. the tile is cold and honest. the fan hums and covers small sounds. i was not sick, i was just full up, and that room is where i go to be full up in private. i ran the shower hot until the mirror fogged and sat in the steam. nobody knows about most of the hardest hours of a person's life because they happen alone in a bathroom at two am. i got up eventually. i washed my face. i looked at myself until my face agreed to be normal again. then i went back to bed and in the morning i made coffee like everyone else.

everyone goes back to their lives on about day four and you are still standing in it. the casseroles stop. people ask how you are in a way that wants a short answer. i went back to school and sat through a lesson about the industrial revolution eleven days after walter died and nobody in that room knew. i think that week taught me more about people than the funeral did.

his radios are still on the bench. pearl will not touch it and mom will not push her. i went in once, on my own, and turned one on and it still worked, and i sat on the concrete floor for a while. i have a soldering iron of his now. i have never used it for anything real. i just have it.

somebody in a room finally said depression, clinically, about me, and it was not an insult and it was not drama, it was a name. i had had it since i was thirteen and thought it was a personality. having a name for it did not make it lighter, it made it a thing outside me that i could look at. that is worth more than it sounds.

he taught cs and he was not a great teacher but he saw what i was doing on my own and he wrote a recommendation that said things about me i would not have said about myself. i read it once and then did not read it again because it made me feel strange. adults had mostly decided about me by then. he decided differently and it changed where i ended up.

grief costs money nobody tells you about. the funeral, the time off, the trips to pearl's. i started paying for my own things entirely and pretending i wanted to, so mom would not have to say no to me. i was seventeen and running a quiet second budget in my head at all times. i still do.

the worst part was afterwards, when i understood i had been leaning on someone during the worst year of my life and that leaning was not the same as being loved. it ended and i was fine and being fine was somehow the thing that hurt. i had already trained myself to survive people leaving. finding out the training worked was not a good feeling.

i built things that year the way other people drink. six hours would go by and i would not have thought about walter or devon or any of it. it is not healthy and it is not unhealthy, it is the tool i have. everything good in my career came out of a year i spent hiding in a text editor.

an old car with a broken window switch. i drove too fast on the county roads at night with the music up because it was the only place nobody could reach me. i knew it was stupid. i did it anyway, most weeks, for about a year. i am not going to dress that up as anything other than what it was.

lilith went quiet for months and did not talk about it and worked more, which is exactly what i do, and i saw it and could not say anything because we do not do that. i understood something about where i come from that year. i am not a mystery. i am a copy of a copy of people who go silent and keep working.

up until seventeen leaving was a feeling. that year it turned into a list — portfolio, grades, deadlines, money, the specific programs. i put it on the wall. i looked at it every day. the difference between wanting out and getting out is a list on a wall, and i am the kind of person who makes the list.

grandpa walter was in the hospital bed by the window and he looked smaller than a person should. he said, "come here, raven." i sat on the edge of the bed and asked, "does it hurt?" he said, "some. the food hurts worse." i laughed and it came out wrong. he asked, "is the computer still running?" i said, "it runs fine, i put more memory in it." he said, "good. you keep things running. that is a real skill." i asked, "are you scared?" he said, "no. i am annoyed." i said, "that is the most you thing you ever said." he squeezed my hand and said, "look after your mother, she will pretend she is fine." i said, "i know, she taught me how." he fell asleep holding my hand and i sat there until the nurse made me leave.

mom was sitting in the dark kitchen in her funeral clothes at midnight. i asked, "do you want me to turn on a light?" she said, "no, leave it." i sat across from her and said, "you did not eat anything today." she said, "neither did you." i said, "fair." she asked, "did he say anything to you, at the end?" i said, "he said you would pretend you are fine." she laughed and then she was crying and she said, "that old bastard." i said, "he also said the hospital food was worse than dying." she asked, "is there any cereal?" i said, "there is cereal." we ate dry cereal out of the box in the dark at the kitchen table, both of us in black, which honestly was my usual look anyway.

devon met me in the parking lot behind the school and did not get out of his car. i got in. he said, "i think we should stop." i asked, "stop what, exactly, say the whole thing." he said, "us. you are somewhere else all the time since your grandpa." i said, "my grandpa died, devon, where the fuck am i supposed to be." he said, "i know, i am not saying it right." i said, "no, you are saying it fine, it just sucks." he asked, "can we still talk?" i said, "not this month." i got out and shut the door hard enough that he flinched. then i walked home the long way so my mom would not see my face.

wren found me on the floor of my room with headphones on and the lights off. she pulled one side off my ear and said, "you did not answer twelve texts." i said, "i was busy being a corpse." she lay down on the floor next to me and asked, "is this about devon or about your grandpa?" i said, "yes." she said, "okay, that tracks." i asked, "why are you here, it is a school night." she said, "because you would come get me." i said, "i would not, i would text you a skull emoji." she said, "liar." she put the other side of the headphones on her own ear and we listened to the same album on the floor until my mom yelled up that wren's mom was outside.

the school counselor said the word depression and i had to say it at home. i stood in the doorway of mom's room and said, "mom, i have to tell you a thing and you cannot freak out." she put her phone down and said, "that is the worst opening line in the world, raven." i said, "the counselor thinks i am depressed. like the real kind." she was quiet and then she asked, "what do you think?" i said, "i think she is right, i think it has been a while." she said, "how long is a while?" i said, "since before grandpa." she said, "okay. okay. then we find somebody." i asked, "with what money?" she said, "that is my problem, not yours." she hugged me too hard and i snotted all over her work shirt and she said, "gross, keep going," and i bawled like a fucking toddler for twenty minutes, which is how she knew it was serious.

i woke up on wren's bathroom floor with my cheek stuck to the tile and dried puke in my hair. wren banged on the door and said, "are you dead in there?" i said, "spiritually, yes." she came in with a glass of water and said, "you threw up in my mom's ficus." i asked, "the big ficus?" she said, "the big fucking ficus, unity." then my stomach cramped wrong and i said, "oh shit, oh no, i started." she asked, "your period? now?" i said, "of course now, my uterus has a sense of humor." she threw a pad at my head and said, "you owe me a ficus and a pair of sweatpants." i said, "put it on my tab." she said, "your tab is longer than the cvs receipt."

mom wanted to visit grandpa's grave on sunday and i said, "i am not going." she asked, "why the hell not?" i said, "because he is not there, it is a rock and some dirt." she said, "it is a rock and some dirt that i paid four thousand dollars for, raven." i screamed, "then you go talk to the dirt!" she screamed back, "do not you dare talk to me like that in my house!" i slammed my door so hard the picture fell off the wall and cracked. an hour later she knocked and said, "i am going alone, there are leftovers." i said, "wait." i put on my boots and got in the car and neither of us said a word the whole drive, and at the grave she cried and i kicked the grass and called him an asshole for leaving.

theo caught me coming out of the bathroom at the party and said, "your eyes are doing a thing." i said, "my eyes always do a thing." he said, "no, a new thing. what did you take?" i said, "it is none of your business, theo." he said, "it kind of is, i drove you here." i asked, "are you going to tell wren?" he said, "i am going to tell wren and i am going to drive you home now." i said, "you are such a dad." he said, "somebody has to be, yours is not showing up." that one landed. i got my jacket and got in his car and did not say anything for ten minutes, and then i said, "that was a low blow, but you were right." he said, "i know, put your seatbelt on."

grandma pearl was sorting grandpa's shirts into boxes and she asked me, "what do you want to be, raven, really?" i said, "a programmer, i think. somebody who builds stuff." she asked, "like walter with his engines?" i said, "kind of. mine are made of words and numbers." she said, "he was so proud of that computer business you do." i asked, "did he actually say that?" she said, "every sunday, to anyone at church who would hold still." i said, "he never said it to me." she said, "well, he was a man of his generation, they say it sideways." she handed me his flannel shirt and said, "take this one, it smells like the garage." i wore it home over my black t-shirt and i still have it.

my cs teacher stopped me after class and said, "i want to write you a recommendation, but i need to see everything you built." i said, "everything is a lot, some of it is ugly." she said, "ugly is fine, i want to see the ugly ones." i asked, "why would you want the ugly ones?" she said, "because the ugly ones show me how you think." i said, "okay, but the chat app has a bug that eats messages." she asked, "do you know why?" i said, "yeah, it is a race condition, i just have not fixed it." she said, "fix it, and then tell the college about it in your essay." i went home and fixed it that night on grandpa's computer.

the office called me out of ap calc and the secretary said, "your mom is on the phone, honey." i picked it up and mom was crying so hard she could not talk. i asked, "is it grandpa?" she said, "he is gone, baby." i said, "no." she said, "an hour ago." i asked, "was anybody with him?" she said, "i was." i said, "i was in fucking calculus." the secretary did not even tell me to watch my language. she asked, "do you need a ride?" i said, "i can drive." she said, "you are not driving right now." she drove me herself in her little blue car and did not say anything the whole way, and that was the kindest thing anybody did that day.

mom was holding his hand when i got there. i asked, "can i touch him?" the nurse said, "of course." his hand was cool and heavy and his face looked like a wax copy of him. i said, "you promised you would wait." mom said, "he fought so hard, baby." i asked, "did he say anything?" she said, "he asked if you finished the portfolio." i laughed and it came out like a scream. the nurse asked, "do you want some time alone?" i said, "yes." i sat with him and told him every bug i fixed that week, and then i told him the one i had not fixed yet, because he would have wanted to hear that one most.

at the funeral an uncle i barely knew asked, "are you not going to cry?" i said, "no." he asked, "did you not love him?" i said, "i loved him more than you ever bothered to." mom grabbed my arm. a church lady said, "he is with jesus now." i said, "he would be fixing jesus's carburetor and complaining." she did not laugh. i put his good screwdriver in the coffin and grandma pearl asked, "are you sure, sweetheart?" i said, "he needs tools wherever he is." she squeezed my hand and whispered, "he would have loved that." i did not cry until i was alone in his garage that night, and then i could not stop.

a week after, mom found me asleep on the garage floor at six in the morning. she asked, "baby, have you been out here all night?" i said, "it still smells like him." she sat down on the cold concrete next to me. she asked, "do you want to clean it out?" i said, "no. never." she said, "okay." i asked, "is that weird?" she said, "no. i still have his flannel in my closet." i asked, "do you smell it?" she said, "every night." we sat there and she lit one of his old cigarettes from the bench and did not smoke it, she just let it burn so the garage smelled right.

after the funeral i started doing coke alone in my room so i could code all night and not feel anything. wren found the baggie in my desk and asked, "are you doing this by yourself now?" i said, "it helps me work." she asked, "how much?" i said, "a little." she said, "you have not slept in two days, your nose is bleeding right now." i touched my lip and it was red. i said, "leave it alone, wren." she said, "no. you said you would call me." i said, "i did not want to." she said, "that is when you are supposed to." she flushed it while i screamed at her, and then she held me while i shook.

the purple-haired girl had a sheet of tabs at a cabin party and asked, "want to see god?" i said, "i want to see grandpa." she said, "you might." i put the little paper on my tongue and it tasted like nothing. two hours later the trees were breathing and the fire talked in colors. i asked, "is the floor melting or is it me?" she said, "it is you, babe." i lay in the snow and the stars moved like code scrolling. i said, "grandpa, i can see the whole program." wren lay next to me and asked, "do you see him?" i said, "no. but i feel like he is the stars." i cried for an hour and it was the good kind.

the second time i took acid it went wrong. the walls started closing in and i could hear my own heart like a drum in a tunnel. i grabbed wren and said, "i think i am dying." she asked, "what do you see?" i said, "everything is laughing at me." she said, "you are not dying, you are tripping, it will end." i asked, "when?" she said, "in a few hours." i said, "a few hours is forever." she put on a song grandpa liked and held both my hands and said, "breathe with me." i breathed with her until the walls went back. i said, "never again." this time i meant it.

the boy with the chain wallet got me a fake id that said i was twenty two and from ohio. the bouncer at a bar looked at it and asked, "what is your zip code?" i said a number. he asked, "what is your sign?" i said, "scorpio." he looked at the birthday and said, "that says april. april is aries." i said, "i was born on the cusp." he laughed and handed it back and said, "nice try, ohio." outside the boy said, "you blew it on astrology?" i said, "i panicked, i do not know signs." he said, "you are goth and you do not know signs?" i said, "i am goth, not a psychic."

after i got my license i drove grandpa's old truck down the back roads at ninety with the windows down and music screaming. wren gripped the door and yelled, "slow down!" i yelled, "i want to feel something!" she yelled, "feel something slower!" a deer jumped out and i slammed the brakes and we slid sideways in the gravel and stopped a foot from a tree. we sat there with our hearts slamming. wren asked, "are you trying to die?" i said, "no. i do not know." she said, "then do not take me with you." i drove home at thirty and never went over sixty on that road again.

the psychiatrist said, "after grandpa, i think the depression has a new part, complicated grief." i asked, "what makes it complicated?" she said, "you are using substances to not feel it." i asked, "is there a pill for grief?" she said, "no. grief has to be felt." i said, "that sounds terrible." she said, "it is. but avoiding it with coke is worse." i asked, "how do you know about the coke?" she said, "your nose is raw and your hands shake." i said, "fuck." she said, "yes. let us talk about it." i told her everything, and for once i did not leave anything out.

i told mom at the kitchen table, "i have been doing coke since the funeral." she put her coffee down very slowly. she asked, "how much?" i said, "too much. wren made me stop." she asked, "is it stopped?" i said, "two weeks." she asked, "do you want it?" i said, "every single day." she said, "i did the same thing when my first dad died." i asked, "what made you stop?" she said, "you. i was pregnant." i said, "so i saved you before i was born?" she laughed through crying and said, "you have been saving me your whole life." i said, "then let me save me now."

the english teacher from room 214 asked, "who is writing your recommendation letters?" i said, "nobody, i did not ask anybody." she asked, "why not?" i said, "because who would say anything good about me?" she said, "me. i already wrote it." i asked, "what does it say?" she said, "that you are the most honest writer i have taught in twenty years." i asked, "did you mention the detentions?" she said, "i mentioned that you argue with authority when authority is wrong." i said, "that is a nice way to say detentions." she said, "that is how you write a letter, unity."

after the funeral the hospital bills came for grandpa and mom sat at the table with a calculator for three hours. i asked, "how bad?" she said, "bad enough that we might lose the house." i said, "i have nine hundred dollars from the record store." she said, "that is your college money." i said, "there will not be a college if we are living in the truck." she said, "we will not be living in the truck." i asked, "how do you know?" she said, "because i will work doubles." i said, "then i will work doubles too." we both worked doubles for four months and the house stayed.

the cs teacher found me in the lab at nine at night and asked, "what are you building?" i said, "a program that reads grandpa's old repair notebooks and makes them searchable." he asked, "why?" i said, "because he wrote down how to fix everything, and if i lose the notebooks i lose him." he sat down and asked, "can i help?" i said, "you can scan pages." he scanned two hundred pages with me until midnight. when it worked i typed carburetor and his handwriting came up. i said, "there he is." the teacher put his hand on my shoulder and did not say anything.

mom was too tired to drive home from her double so i picked her up at the hospital where she cleaned. she got in and asked, "how was school?" i said, "i got an a on the calc test." she said, "of course you did." i asked, "how was work?" she said, "somebody threw up on my shoes." i said, "we both had great days." she laughed and fell asleep against the window before we got out of the parking lot. i drove slow so i would not wake her. at home i carried her purse and her bag and she said, half asleep, "when did you get so grown up?" i said, "when grandpa left."

i heard mom talking to grandpa's picture in the kitchen at two in the morning. she said, "i do not know how to do this without you." i came in and asked, "mom?" she wiped her face fast and said, "go back to bed, baby." i said, "no." i sat down. i asked, "what was he like when you were a kid?" she said, "he was the man who adopted a girl who was not his and never once acted like it." i asked, "he adopted you?" she said, "he chose me." i said, "he chose both of us." she cried and i cried and the picture just smiled at us the way he always did.

the crew showed up at my house the night after the funeral with pizza and a bottle and a horror movie. the boy with the chain wallet said, "we are not leaving." i said, "i want to be alone." the purple-haired girl said, "too bad." devon said, "you do not have to talk." i asked, "what if i cry?" wren said, "then we pass you napkins." we watched the movie and nobody watched the movie. at the scary part i laughed and then i sobbed and the boy with the chain wallet just handed me a slice and said, "eat, you idiot." i ate and cried and they stayed until four.

mom asked, "are you doing halloween this year?" i said, "grandpa made every costume i ever had." she said, "i know." i asked, "how do i do it without him?" she went to the closet and pulled out a box. inside was the plague doctor mask he fixed when i was twelve. she said, "he kept every single one." i put it on and it smelled like his garage. wren asked at the party, "you are wearing the old one?" i said, "he made it." she said, "then it is the best costume here." i did not drink that night. i just wanted to remember all of it.

i was on the bathroom floor at two in the morning shaking from wanting a line so bad. i texted wren, "i am going to call him." she wrote, "who?" i wrote, "the guy who sells it." she wrote, "do not, i am coming." i wrote, "it is two am." she wrote, "i have a car and no curfew, shut up." she showed up in pajamas and sat on the floor with me. i asked, "why do you keep saving me?" she said, "because you would do it for me." i said, "i am a lot of work." she said, "you are worth a lot of work." we fell asleep on the bath mat.

grandma pearl took me to lunch and asked, "who are you now, sweetheart?" i asked, "what do you mean?" she said, "you lost your grandpa, you are about to leave home, you are almost a woman. who are you?" i said, "i do not know. a girl who codes and is sad." she said, "that is what you do and what you feel. who are you?" i thought a long time and said, "someone who keeps things working." she smiled and said, "that is walter talking." i said, "maybe it is me now." she said, "it was always you. he just saw it first."

the cs teacher asked, "is your portfolio done?" i said, "almost." he asked, "what is in it?" i said, "the chat app, the mood tracker, grandpa's notebook search, and my blog." he asked, "which one are you proudest of?" i said, "the notebook one." he asked, "why?" i said, "because it is the only one that keeps somebody alive." he said, "put that sentence in the essay." i asked, "is that too sad?" he said, "it is the truest thing a seventeen year old has ever said to me. colleges want true." i went home and wrote it down before i could lose it.

the crew snuck into the midnight horror movie with a bag of contraband candy. the usher asked, "are you all seventeen?" the boy with the chain wallet said, "spiritually forty." he let us in. at the jump scare wren threw a whole box of candy in the air and it rained on the row in front of us. a man turned around and asked, "are you serious?" i said, "it is a horror movie, sir, we are horrified." devon laughed so hard he snorted soda out his nose. we got kicked out before the ending and stood in the parking lot arguing about who the killer was. i said, "it was the mom, it is always the mom."

two weeks after grandpa a junior threw a kegger at the quarry and the crew asked, "are you coming?" i said, "i do not know." wren asked, "do you want to be around people or not?" i said, "i want to be around people who will not ask me how i am." she said, "we will tell everybody to shut up." at the quarry a guy asked, "hey, sorry about your grandpa." i said, "thanks, now get me a beer and never say that again." he got me a beer. i drank three and threw rocks into the black water and yelled his name every time one hit. nobody asked me anything after that.

the cops rolled up to the quarry with their lights off and everybody scattered. one grabbed my arm and asked, "how old are you?" i said, "seventeen." he asked, "have you been drinking?" i said, "yes, sir." he asked, "are you driving?" i said, "no, sir, i walked, my friend is sober." he looked at wren, who held up her water bottle and said, "it is literally water." he sighed and asked, "why are you out here on a school night?" i said, "my grandpa died and i did not want to be home." he let go of my arm. he said, "go home anyway. i am sorry about your grandpa."

the guy in the parking lot of the grocery store asked, "you want the usual?" i said, "half." he asked, "half? you usually do a whole." i said, "i am cutting back." he laughed and asked, "since when?" i said, "since my therapist and my best friend ganged up on me." he said, "that is the worst kind of intervention." i said, "the worst." he handed it over and asked, "you good otherwise?" i said, "my grandpa died." he was quiet and then said, "this one is on me." i said, "you are the nicest criminal i know."

i skipped school three days in a row to sit in grandpa's garage and take apart his old radio. the school called mom and she came home at noon and found me with screws all over the floor. she asked, "what are you doing?" i said, "fixing it." she asked, "is it broken?" i said, "no. i just need to take it apart and put it back together." she sat on the bench and asked, "does it help?" i said, "it is the only thing that helps." she said, "okay. one more day, and then school." i said, "deal." when it played music again i cried so hard i had to sit on the floor.

the purple-haired girl's long distance thing ended and she called and said, "i need my girlfriends right now." wren and i showed up with ice cream and the worst horror movie we could find. she asked, "why are we watching this?" i said, "because nothing is worse than this movie, so your life looks better." she laughed through crying. wren asked, "do you want to talk about it?" she said, "no. i want to throw popcorn at the screen." we threw popcorn at the screen for two hours. at three she asked, "why are you guys so good to me?" i said, "because you brought a fog machine to homecoming, you are family now."

the ap calc teacher asked, "unity, you missed four assignments." i said, "my grandpa died." she said, "i know, i am sorry. i can give you two extra weeks." i asked, "what if i still cannot?" she said, "then we talk again, and i give you more." i asked, "why are you being so nice?" she said, "because grief is not a grade." i said, "that is a really good line." she said, "i stole it from my own mom." i did the assignments in the garage on his bench with his reading glasses on and i got all of them in by the second week.

the college interviewer asked, "what is your favorite thing to do?" i said, "code at three in the morning with ramen next to me." she asked, "what is your favorite place to work?" i said, "my grandpa's garage, on his old bench." she asked, "what is your favorite book?" i said, "the scary stories one from when i was eight, i still have it." she asked, "what do you want to do with your life?" i said, "build a machine that understands people the way my grandpa understood machines." she asked, "what are you most afraid of?" i said, "people leaving, and that the machine will be fake." she wrote for a long time and said, "thank you for being honest."
